lines.note: Narawasu concerns habitual practice. Iy begins the example ii-narawasu, something habitually said; the past form -aita preserves historical s-row i-onbin.
Completes the expression for something current as a proverb or familiar saying. The Japanese example's division after Iy is physical, not an added lexical boundary.
Completes dito commum, a common saying. This is still the explanation of Iy narauaſu, not the following noun entry.
The noun narawashi means custom. The short entry is distinguished from the verb above and the attributive form below.

runs.text: Couſa de cuſtume, ou que ſe acustu

lines.note: Narawashi no describes something customary or habitual. The final Portuguese word continues on the next row without a printed hyphen.
Completes acustuma and gives an example about the body being shaped by habit. The Portuguese translation starts with the article O at the right edge.

runs.text: corpo he conforme ao que o custumão.

lines.note: Completes the body's conformity to what it is accustomed to. The historical custumão is retained rather than replaced by a modern verb form.
Narashi, alternatively kakezao, is a bamboo or wooden rail used for clothing. Latin l introduces the Japanese synonym.
Completes the clothes-rail gloss. The scan reads vestidos, not coestidos; upright X. supplies the regional label and is outside the italic Portuguese.
This narashi means rehearsal, such as for a play or dance. The source's bailo is preserved rather than modernized.
Narasu first means to level or smooth. Giuo begins the example 'level the ground,' with gi representing the relevant Japanese voiced syllable.
Completes the ground-leveling example, then introduces rehearsing a dance as another sense. Its Japanese illustration follows on the next row.
Odori wo narasu illustrates rehearsing a dance. The initial V and the historical ſ are retained; this is an example sentence, not a typeface-toggle term within Portuguese prose.

This narasu means causing something to sound. The damaged vowel after R is read as e in Reiuo, supported by the surviving curved strokes and the bell translation below; the printed principal form ita is not expanded.
Completes rei wo narasu, to ring the small bell. The Portuguese confirms that the example concerns sound, not rehearsal or leveling.

runs.text: Certo achar de Nara que ſe faz

lines.note: Narazuke is a pickle associated with Nara. The source reads achar, not alhar; Nara occurs inside the Portuguese explanation and is recorded as a whole-word typeface-review term.

Completes the description as something made in place of konomono, pickled accompaniments. Conomono is embedded in Portuguese prose; the visible italic setting is retained and the whole term is flagged for optional font review.
Naruru means becoming accustomed. The grammatical explanation begins by requiring a verb stem before it; the close printed Querantes is retained rather than silently respaced.

runs.text: de ſi a raiz dos verbos com que ſe ajunta, &

lines.note: Explains the construction with the stem of the verb to which naruru is attached. The Portuguese sentence and its grammatical condition continue below.

runs.text: então ſignifica ſer acuſtumado a fazer o que ſig-

lines.note: The compound then means being accustomed to doing what the preceding stem denotes. The final sig- begins significa on the next row.

runs.text: nifica a raiz do verbo. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the grammatical explanation and illustrates it with minaruru, becoming used to seeing. The Portuguese translation starts at the right edge.
Completes 'accustomed to seeing,' then introduces becoming familiar with someone as another sense. No modernization of acustumado is made.
The example hito ni naruru means becoming familiar with a person. The scan reads Fitoni with t, correcting the draft's Ficoni.
Narenareshii describes familiarity. The example begins with the same adjective divided at the physical line ending, and its concessive framing follows below.

Completes the adjective in a concessive expression about familiar speech. The Portuguese is Posto que seja, 'although it may be'; the damaged t was omitted by OCR, while its supplied short-s convention is retained.

runs.text: falar como quem tem muita familiaridade, &

lines.note: Explains speaking as someone with great familiarity. The scan supports familiaridade, correcting the draft's intrusive t in familtaridade.
Completes the concessive translation: despite familiarity and conversation, nevertheless, and so on. The source's conuerſação retains historical u for consonantal v.
Nare no hate concerns the outcome of a person's conduct. The source prefers Nareru fate; the scan corrects both Melis to Meliùs and Nateru to Nareru. The good-or-bad contrast continues after a comma.

runs.text: ou mao em que hum pàra por ſuas obras.

lines.note: Completes the outcome as good or bad, determined by one's deeds. The grave in pàra is retained as printed rather than normalized to modern orthography.
The example expresses a wish to see how that person ends up. De- begins the Portuguese Desejo on the next row.

runs.text: ſejo ſaber como acaba aquelle homem. Vſaſe cõ

lines.note: Completes 'I wish to know how that man ends.' The usage explanation starts with Vſaſe and abbreviated cõ, continued without a hyphen below.

runs.text: mummente acerca de homẽs de ruim vida.

lines.note: Completes commummente and says the expression is generally used about people leading bad lives. The nasal abbreviation in homẽs remains unexpanded.
Nari is defined as manner, shape, or appearance. This noun is distinct from both sound and the grammatical copula in the neighboring entries.
This nari means noise or sound. The example begins by quieting the noise; xiz- continues the Japanese verb across the row boundary.
Completes shizumete kiku, listening after quieting the noise. The Portuguese mentions making the people silent; its printed agente remains unseparated.
Adds quieting the commotion as an alternative explanation. This continues the sound example rather than introducing another sense of appearance.
The written copula nari is equated with de gozaru, 'to be.' The upright Japanese equivalent and i, are separated from the italic explanation; a comment on sentence-final usage begins here.

runs.text: vezes não ſerue mais que de elegancia cõ que

lines.note: The compilers say that nari sometimes serves only as an elegant way to end a written sentence. The description continues below and is reported as their grammatical analysis.

runs.text: ſe a caba algũa oração da eſcritura. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the discussion of ending a written sentence, then starts the example Yomiqeru nari. The draft's narrow separation a caba is retained as a spacing caveat rather than silently regularized.
Completes Yomiqeru nari, rendered by the source as 'read.' The Portuguese Leo has no supplied modern accent; the Japanese example illustrates the literary copula.
The verb naru means becoming. Its first example begins hadaka ni naru, becoming naked, with naru divided across the row boundary.
Completes becoming naked and adds teki ni naru, becoming an enemy. The final Portuguese Fazer continues reflexively on the next row.
Completes 'become an enemy,' then introduces hitotsu ni naru, becoming one. A visible word space separates Fitotçuni and naru, unlike the draft's joined form.

runs.text: em hum corpo. ¶ Item, Poder. Vt,

lines.note: Completes becoming one body. The entry then gives the possibility sense of naru and starts the negative construction xeide naranu.

runs.text: Não ſe pode deixar de fazer.

lines.note: Completes the expression that one cannot leave the action undone. The Portuguese explains its necessity-like effect rather than a literal transformation.
This distinct naru means sounding. Its example names a bell and a conch, with nado divided at the end of the row.
Completes 'bells, conches, and so forth sound.' The scan reads Soar o ſino, correcting OCR Scar o ſimo; the long ſ is retained.
Nariagaru means rising to greatness or status. The line ends with a hyphen after no-, not the draft's period; nobre is completed below.
Completes the rise from low status to nobility or eminence. This is the social-advancement sense, distinct from rising sound below.
The noun names rising to greatness. Ano fi- begins the example about a person newly elevated in status.
Completes the Japanese statement about that person's rise. The scan prints homem as one word, correcting the OCR's ho mem.
The translation says that the person has newly become great. It completes the noun example, without adding a modern pejorative sense not stated here.
This homographic verb concerns sound rising or being heard above. The historical aleuantarſe is retained with u.
Completes sounding in a high place, then begins an example about thunder. Tçune- continues tsune ni on the next row.
Thunder rises and descends in the cited Heike passage. The upright Feiq. is the citation label; the italic book reference continues below.

runs.text: 1. Os trouoẽs ora ſoauão em cima no mõ-

lines.note: Book 1 precedes the translation of thunder sounding above on the mountain. A small terminal hyphen is read after the abbreviated mõ-, continuing monte below.
Completes monte and contrasts the thunder sounding below. The upward/downward contrast explains the two Japanese verbs in the example.
Narikakaru means that something is partly made or in the process of becoming. The source's mea is preserved rather than modernized to meia.
Adds 'begun' as the alternative explanation. This continuation belongs to the verb, before the separate noun Naricacari below.
The noun narikakari means form or manner. It is a separate entry from the preceding verb meaning to be partly made.
Narikawarasu is causative: making people change. The object is completed below; the printed principal forms retain the historical causative pattern.

The example concerns turning bad people into good ones. Peßoas is weakly impressed, especially e and o; their faint remnants and the visible spacing support this reading rather than peßas. Acuninuo corrects OCR Acumnuo.

runs.text: Fazer mudar os maos ẽ virtuoſos

lines.note: Completes nari kawarasuru and translates it as changing the wicked into virtuous people. The nasal abbreviation ẽ is retained; no conjectural terminal punctuation is supplied at the crowded right rule.
Narikawaru means changing into something else. The scan clearly supplies Naricauari, correcting the draft's Vaticauari; the second Portuguese verb is divided.

runs.text: darſe hũa couſa em outra. Vt,

lines.note: Completes mudar-se and begins the example 'wood into stone.' The historical spelling Qiua represents ki wa, while ixini is ishi ni.

runs.text: O pao ſe conuerteo em pedra.

lines.note: Completes the transformation of wood into stone. The translation supports narikawatta; the source's conuerteo is not modernized.
Narikaeru is explained as turning back in one's religious affiliation. The scan includes the i after Nar, absent from OCR Narcayeri.
Completes the reference to the religion one professes. The wording concerns religious reversal, not merely returning to a physical place.
Narikodaru describes fruit hanging from a tree. The Portuguese dependurada is divided, and the following row also contains an unrelated displaced fragment at its far right.

The main text completes fruit hanging from the tree. The far-right (honra, &c. belongs to the following entry's decline in status and honor; it is encoded as a displaced segment, not attached to the fruit gloss.
Narikudaru means declining in status; the displaced honra, &c. on the preceding row adds honor and similar standing. The scan supplies deſcaindo with n, correcting OCR deſcaido.
This narikudaru concerns sound descending or sounding below. The weak rounded letter is read as o in ou, not the draft's capital C; decer is retained as printed.
Completes 'sound below,' matching the descent of thunder in the earlier example. The physical continuation is not merged with the next noun entry.
Narikuse is a natural disposition or habitual peculiarity. Fi- begins hito no narikuse; the tilde remains on the printed carrier in Feiçaõ.
Completes the example about a person's habitual nature. The Portuguese offers disposition, custom, or manner as related explanations.
Completes the description as someone's natural manner. The contracted dalguem is preserved without introducing modern punctuation or an accent.
Narihatsuru means coming completely to an end or reaching utter ruin. The example that follows supplies the unfavorable interpretation.
The speaker has no one to rely on and is utterly reduced. Cocorobo- begins kokorobosoku, describing forlornness, across the physical division.

Completes the feeling of forlornness. The citation is visibly italic here. Its damaged numeral is provisionally read as 18: 8 is clear, with a faint possible 1 immediately before it; 8 alone remains a nonblocking alternative.

runs.text: tendo a quem ſe encoſtar, nem de quem ſe valer

lines.note: The Portuguese explains having nobody to lean on or obtain help from. This is the translation of tanomu katanaku, not an independent moral statement.

runs.text: perdido de todo eſtaua triſte, & acanhado.

lines.note: Completes the translation as utterly lost, sad, and constrained or dejected. The printed historical eſtaua is retained.
The second example means ending up in a miserable condition. The grave on ù is retained instead of substituting a modern long-vowel mark.
Completes the condition as miserable. This short line belongs to the preceding example and retains its separate physical crop.
Narihôdai is referred to the preferred form Narixidai. The meaning is according to what can be done, completed below; the circumflex in the headword is retained.

runs.text: for poßiuel, ou cõforme ao que ſe poder fazer.

lines.note: Completes the definition as whatever is possible or practicable. The source's cõforme and poder are preserved rather than expanded or grammatically modernized.

runs.text: Couſa difficultoſa de ſer, ou deſe fazer.

lines.note: Narigatai describes something difficult to be or to accomplish. The close deſe is retained as printed, and the entry is complete on this line.

runs.text: O não ſe lograr a fruita ſaindo mur-

lines.note: Narigane first concerns fruit failing to develop properly. The scan corrects fraita to fruita and the terminal period to a hyphen dividing murcha.
Completes the description of withered, shriveled, imperfect fruit. A paragraph mark then introduces a transferred human application.

runs.text: permet. Se diz de hũa peßoa que nãoſaye como

lines.note: The abbreviation permet. introduces metaphorical usage: a person who does not turn out as expected. The close nãoſaye is retained rather than silently respaced.

runs.text: ſe eſpera, mas fica como aleijada ſem eſpiritos

lines.note: Continues with the source's disparaging comparison to an impaired person lacking spirit. The scan supports aleijada with i, missing in OCR alejada; the characterization is attributed to the historical gloss.
Completes the lack of knowledge and supplies an example using Narigane de gozaru. The nasal abbreviation nẽ and the Japanese word spacing are preserved.
Narimono here concerns fruit-bearing produce. The example identifies a tree of that kind; the Portuguese translation starts at the far right.
Completes 'a tree that bears fruit.' The printed unaccented da and historical fruito remain unchanged.

runs.text: Couſa que ſoa, ou ſe tange.

lines.note: This distinct narimono means something that sounds or is played, such as an instrument. The separate Nari below is the next-page catchword, not part of this gloss.
The signature is Y y 2. The capital Y is badly impressed, with the detached right arm still visible; it is not the OCR r. The lower-case y and numeral 2 are clear.
The far-right upright catchword anticipates Nariſagari on f0356. It is spatially distinct from the signature and is not part of the preceding definition.
